items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got into Ellington because of the popular songs that he wrote and recorded... I remember one of the first ones that I ever bought was Sophisticated Lady... I started going really to hear the Basie band... listening to Ellington and Basie, particularly... I was sitting opposite the Ellington band..

ctx.x: Were the other bands – was it easier for the other bands to be heard because they were white?

Oh yes, definitely. I remember that Ellington was very seldom heard on the radio. All of these black musicians were not heard much. I got into Ellington because of the popular songs that he wrote and recorded. I remember one of the first ones that I ever bought was Sophisticated Lady, on Brunswick. The path led, of course, into other Ellington music. By the time I graduated from Horace Mann, I had quite a few Ellington Brunswicks. items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: Delaunay and Panassié worked very closely together interviewing American musicians who got to France and these Americans like Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter and even Armstrong himself and eventually Duke Ellington in the late 30s, were extremely important in terms of the information that they furnish

ctx.x: Yes certainly it was before LPs, but the idea of him spreading through recording.

Well that’s absolutely true, because people got to know the history of jazz that way, through LPs even more than those 78s that I just talked about, that started around 1940. And the fact that it was an organized series meant that people knew that they could expect another release the following month, and that way they were on the lookout. And the annotations that I wrote for the 78 RPM albums were the first group of written documentation of the careers of some of these performers, because before that there…

rather special reason that I didn’t catch on to at first, which was that the American jazz records that got released abroad tended to stay in the catalogues. They didn’t sell very widely and the record business was smaller in Europe than it was in America, and because they stayed in the catalogues they were there for reference as more and more people got interested in the historical recordings of the 1920s and early 30s.
